# Google Meet's AI Notetaker Is Getting Screenshots Soon — What Changes for You

You sat through a meeting, slides flashing past, and now you're trying to remember what was on slide seven. Sound familiar? The good news: that problem is about to get smaller. Google has confirmed that **"Take notes for me"** in Google Meet is getting an upgrade soon — and one of the biggest changes is exactly what most people have been missing.

Here's what the feature does today, what's coming, and how to use it well in the meantime.

## What's happening

Google Meet's "Take notes for me" is an **AI notetaker** — think of it as a silent meeting assistant that listens along and writes things down. Soon, it'll do something extra: capture **screenshots** of what's shared on screen during the meeting and drop them straight into your notes document.

That sounds small, but it's actually a big deal. Right now, the AI can tell you *"Sarah showed the Q3 chart"* — but it can't show you the chart itself. After the update, the actual visual lands in your notes alongside the transcript. No more guessing what was on slide seven.

There's no exact launch date yet, but Google has confirmed it's coming soon.

## What the feature does today

Until the update lands, here's how "Take notes for me" works:

- Joins the call as a clearly labeled participant — everyone sees a notification
- **Transcribes** (writes out, word for word) what everyone says
- Produces a short summary at the end, including suggested **action items** (tasks to follow up on)
- Saves everything to a **Google Doc** (a cloud-based Word-style document) in the organizer's Drive

The feature is part of **Google Workspace** (the paid business and education version of Google's productivity tools), and is powered by Google's **Gemini AI** (Google's family of AI models).

## A few honest trade-offs

Even after screenshots arrive, a couple of things are worth keeping in mind:

- **Audio quality matters.** Background noise, strong accents, or people talking over each other will reduce transcript accuracy — screenshots don't fix that.
- **Summaries are useful, not perfect.** The summary is generated by AI and can miss nuance. Treat it as a starting point, not a final record.
- **It's opt-in.** Every participant is notified when the notetaker joins. There's no secret recording here.

## What this means for you

- **If you attend lots of meetings:** Treat today's notes as a reliable *spoken-word* record, and the upcoming version as a *spoken-word-plus-visuals* record. Either way, pair them with the actual slide deck if you need the full picture.
- **If you run or present meetings:** Your audience will soon be able to re-read what you *said* **and** see what you *showed*. Worth keeping in mind the next time you put something on screen.
- **If you manage a team or Workspace:** It's worth a quick conversation about expectations and privacy. The opt-in notice goes a long way, but people still appreciate being told in advance.
- **If you're just curious:** Try it once on a low-stakes meeting and read the notes afterwards. You'll learn more in five minutes than any article can tell you.

## Wrap-up

"Take notes for me" has always been solid for capturing what was *said*. Soon, it'll be just as useful for capturing what was *shown* — which closes a real gap for most meeting-goers.

**One small step to try today:** Open your last meeting notes doc and notice what's there. Spoken words — captured. The chart from slide 12 — about to be captured too. The upgrade is worth keeping an eye out for.
